lesson_title: Upstairs or Downstairs: Solving Right-Angled Triangles
hook_text: Measure an 86-metre distance out at sea without leaving the cliff. Here's how.
clip_script: Stand in the corner of a room and look diagonally across. Three things around you: the wall in front, the wall beside you, the long diagonal. That is a triangle, and the names depend on where you stand. Facing you — opposite. Beside you — adjacent. The long diagonal — hypotenuse, and it never changes. Now pick only the two sides that matter: the one you know and the one you want. Opposite and hypotenuse means sine. Adjacent and hypotenuse means cosine. Opposite and adjacent means tangent. Done. Then the bit that trips everyone. Where is the unknown sitting? Upstairs, on top of the fraction — multiply. Downstairs, underneath — divide. Twelve loaves for R216: you divide to get one loaf. Same logic. And here is the payoff. You stand on a forty-metre cliff at Hermanus and look down at a boat, twenty-five degrees below the horizontal. Move yourself to the boat — the angle looking up is the same twenty-five, because both horizontals are parallel. Cliff opposite, sea distance adjacent, so tangent. Unknown downstairs, so divide: forty over tan twenty-five. Eighty-five comma seven eight metres. You just measured the sea without getting wet.
visual_style: A room corner morphing into a labelled triangle; a fraction bar with the unknown flipping between upstairs and downstairs; a final wide shot of a cliff, a horizontal dotted line and a boat with the distance ticking out.
pacing: Grounded on the room corner, crisp on the upstairs-downstairs beat, expansive on the cliff.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for elevation, depression and the observer-height trap.
